title: A bivalent Lassa virus mRNA vaccine protects guinea pigs from lethal infection with Lassa virus
abstract: Abstract: Lassa virus (LASV), the causative agent of the life-threatening febrile disease, Lassa fever, remains a major public health concern in West Africa, where hundreds of thousands of infections occur annually. However, no licensed vaccine is currently available, highlighting the urgent need for effective preventive measures. We previously demonstrated that an mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccine expressing LASV glycoprotein precursor (GPC; LASgpc-mRNA-LNP) conferred protection against lethal infection with a recombinant lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus expressing LASV GPC in mice. In this study, we extended our previous work with the aim of evaluating the efficacy of an mRNA-LNP vaccine expressing LASV nucleoprotein (NP; LASnp-mRNA-LNP) and a bivalent vaccine combining LASgpc-mRNA-LNP and LASnp-mRNA-LNP. Using a lethal CBA/N mouse model of infection with ML29, an LASV live-attenuated vaccine candidate encoding LASV GPC and NP, we found that LASgpc-mRNA-LNP and LASnp-mRNA-LNP each conferred protection in the absence of detectable neutralizing antibody responses. We identified LASV GPC- and NP-derived CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell epitope peptides in CBA/N mice and demonstrated that vaccination induced robust antigen-specific T-cell responses. Importantly, the bivalent vaccine provided complete protection against lethal challenge with doses at which monovalent vaccines failed to protect all mice, suggesting a potential dose-sparing benefit of the bivalent formulation. Furthermore, the bivalent vaccine fully protected guinea pigs against lethal challenge with authentic LASV. Together, these findings establish LASV NP, in addition to GPC, as a protective antigen in the mRNA vaccine platform and provide a rationale for developing bivalent mRNA-LNP vaccines to improve protection against Lassa fever. One Sentence Summary A bivalent mRNA-LNP vaccine expressing Lassa virus GPC and NP confers robust protection against lethal Lassa virus infection

source_body_en: Abstract: Lassa virus (LASV), the causative agent of the life-threatening febrile disease, Lassa fever, remains a major public health concern in West Africa, where hundreds of thousands of infections occur annually. However, no licensed vaccine is currently available, highlighting the urgent need for effective preventive measures. We previously demonstrated that an mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccine expressing LASV glycoprotein precursor (GPC; LASgpc-mRNA-LNP) conferred protection against lethal infection with a recombinant lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus expressing LASV GPC in mice. In this study, we extended our previous work with the aim of evaluating the efficacy of an mRNA-LNP vaccine expressing LASV nucleoprotein (NP; LASnp-mRNA-LNP) and a bivalent vaccine combining LASgpc-mRNA-LNP and LASnp-mRNA-LNP. Using a lethal CBA/N mouse model of infection with ML29, an LASV live-attenuated vaccine candidate encoding LASV GPC and NP, we found that LASgpc-mRNA-LNP and LASnp-mRNA-LNP each conferred protection in the absence of detectable neutralizing antibody responses. We identified LASV GPC- and NP-derived CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell epitope peptides in CBA/N mice and demonstrated that vaccination induced robust antigen-specific T-cell responses. Importantly, the bivalent vaccine provided complete protection against lethal challenge with doses at which monovalent vaccines failed to protect all mice, suggesting a potential dose-sparing benefit of the bivalent formulation. Furthermore, the bivalent vaccine fully protected guinea pigs against lethal challenge with authentic LASV. Together, these findings establish LASV NP, in addition to GPC, as a protective antigen in the mRNA vaccine platform and provide a rationale for developing bivalent mRNA-LNP vaccines to improve protection against Lassa fever. title: A transgenic Syrian hamster model for New World hemorrhagic fever mammarenavirus infection
abstract: Mammarenaviruses are endemic in rodent populations worldwide, and their zoonotic transmission can lead to a severe, life-threatening hemorrhagic fever (HF) syndrome. In the Americas, five New World mammarenaviruses (NWMs) are known to cause HF. As vaccines and antiviral therapy options are limited, these viruses pose a significant public health risk and a threat to national security. Research into NWM pathogenesis and the development of effective countermeasures is restricted by the shortage of small-animal models that faithfully reproduce human disease. The pathogenic NWMs use human transferrin receptor 1 (hTfR1) as the receptor for cellular entry. Here, we describe the development of an hTfR1 knock-in golden Syrian hamster line and its susceptibility to Junín virus (JUNV) infection. This transgenic hamster infection model supports TfR1-mediated entry as an essential step in JUNV pathogenesis and provides a novel small-animal model to advance the development of promising host receptor-directed therapies and direct-acting antivirals to improve outcomes in patients with severe disease caused by pathogenic NWMs.

title: Assessment of Edo People Attitude Towards Lassa Fever Diseases Prevention Campaign Programme
abstract: This study examines the attitudes of Edo people in Owan West Local Government Area (LGA) towards Lassa fever prevention campaigns, particularly those broadcast by KU 92.7 FM. Guided by Behaviour Theory and the Health Belief Model, the research explores how awareness and cultural beliefs influence health behaviours. Using a survey method, 398 respondents were selected through stratified and random sampling from a projected population of 112,503. Findings reveal a high level of awareness of Lassa fever, largely due to efforts by health organizations such as the NCDC, Edo State Ministry of Health, and Irrua Specialist Hospital. However, awareness does not consistently lead to preventive action, highlighting gaps in behavioural change. Trust in health professionals was found to enhance campaign effectiveness, though some skepticism persists due to misinformation and cultural beliefs. Radio emerged as a vital communication tool in rural areas, while urban populations relied more on television and social media. Cultural practices, including reliance on herbal remedies and spiritual interpretations of illness, continue to hinder adoption of preventive measures in rural communities. The study concludes that while awareness is widespread, behavioural change remains uneven. It recommends continuous public health messaging and the inclusion of traditional rulers, religious leaders, and community elders in campaign design to improve acceptance and effectiveness. Tailoring communication strategies to local contexts is essential for fostering sustained health behaviour change.

full_text: Co-Infection of Lassa Fever-Malaria (LF) in Endemic Settings: Influence on LF Case Detection in Health Facilities in Ondo State, Nigeria Abstract: In malaria-endemic settings, a positive malaria result may explain fever while Lassa fever (LF) remains clinically possible. This study assessed LF-malaria co-infection, probable missed LF suspicion, and diagnostic delays in selected health facilities in Ondo State, Nigeria. A convergent mixed-methods design combined retrospective review of 463 LF and malaria records from 2021 – 2023 across 10 purposively selected facilities in five high-burden LGAs with nine key-informant interviews. Co-infection required positive LF and malaria laboratory results. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics, chi-square tests and logistic regression; qualitative findings were analysed thematically and integrated through a joint display. All 463 records were purposefully selected as confirmed LF cases. Of these, 297 (64.1%) had positive LF and malaria results. Malaria was suspected in 440 (95.0%) records, and 324 (70.0%) had prior malaria treatment. Probable missed LF suspicion occurred in 103 (22.2%) records. Malaria positivity was associated with missed suspicion (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 5.30, 95% CI 2.13–13.19; p < 0.001). Interviews highlighted symptom overlap, malaria-first reasoning, treatment failure, restricted RT-PCR access, specimen-transport barriers, notification gaps and uneven refresher training. Overall, 386 (83.4%) patients recovered and 53 (11.4%) died; the case-fatality proportion among confirmed LF records was 11.4%. In this selected sample, malaria appeared to mask LF rather than establish an independent cause of mortality. Malaria confirmation should not close the LF detection pathway. Parallel assessment, timely LF specimen collection, reliable transport, effective surveillance communication and practical diagnostic algorithms may support earlier detection. References: [1]. full_text_sections.full_text: Co-Infection of Lassa Fever-Malaria (LF) in Endemic Settings: Influence on LF Case Detection in Health Facilities in Ondo State, Nigeria Abstract: In malaria-endemic settings, a positive malaria result may explain fever while Lassa fever (LF) remains clinically possible. This study assessed LF-malaria co-infection, probable missed LF suspicion, and diagnostic delays in selected health facilities in Ondo State, Nigeria. A convergent mixed-methods design combined retrospective review of 463 LF and malaria records from 2021 – 2023 across 10 purposively selected facilities in five high-burden LGAs with nine key-informant interviews. Co-infection required positive LF and malaria laboratory results. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics, chi-square tests and logistic regression; qualitative findings were analysed thematically and integrated through a joint display. All 463 records were purposefully selected as confirmed LF cases. Of these, 297 (64.1%) had positive LF and malaria results. Malaria was suspected in 440 (95.0%) records, and 324 (70.0%) had prior malaria treatment. Probable missed LF suspicion occurred in 103 (22.2%) records. Malaria positivity was associated with missed suspicion (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 5.30, 95% CI 2.13–13.19; p < 0.001). Interviews highlighted symptom overlap, malaria-first reasoning, treatment failure, restricted RT-PCR access, specimen-transport barriers, notification gaps and uneven refresher training. Overall, 386 (83.4%) patients recovered and 53 (11.4%) died; the case-fatality proportion among confirmed LF records was 11.4%. In this selected sample, malaria appeared to mask LF rather than establish an independent cause of mortality. Malaria confirmation should not close the LF detection pathway. Parallel assessment, timely LF specimen collection, reliable transport, effective surveillance communication and practical diagnostic algorithms may support earlier detection. References: [1].
